text: ITIL's earliest versions, back in the late eighties and through the year 2000, were published as separate books, each covering a cluster of related processes. ITIL v3, in 2007, reorganized that guidance around a Service Lifecycle — five stages: Strategy, Design, Transition, Operation, and Continual Service Improvement — containing twenty-six defined processes in total. That was a real improvement over a loose pile of best practices.

But that lifecycle was still fundamentally linear: strategize, then design, then transition into production, then operate, then look back and improve. By the time ITIL 4 was being developed, organizations were routinely practicing Agile and DevOps — continuous delivery, cross-functional teams, rapid iteration that didn't map cleanly onto finishing one stage before starting the next. ITIL v3's vocabulary had no real place for that.

ITIL 4, released in 2019, replaced the five-stage lifecycle with the broader Service Value System, and replaced the word process with practice. That's not cosmetic — a practice is a set of organizational resources for performing work, which includes the people, skills, and tools involved, not just the steps.

ITIL 4 defines thirty-four practices across three categories — general management, service management, and technical management — replacing v3's twenty-six processes. It also introduced the four dimensions model: any practice has to be viewed through organizations and people, information and technology, partners and suppliers, and value streams and processes, all at once, instead of through process steps alone.

Critically, ITIL 4 explicitly incorporates Agile, DevOps, and Lean thinking into its guidance — something ITIL v3 never did, because those practices weren't yet standard when v3 was written. ITIL 4 treats iterative delivery as normal, not an exception to a sequential lifecycle.
From a rigid five-stage lifecycle of processes, to a flexible system of practices viewed through four dimensions. Next up: a full overview of that Service Value System itself.
